notes:
Centre of mass

  • $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}$ (similarly for $y$, $z$). For an isolated system, the COM moves with constant velocity (or stays at rest); internal forces such as an explosion or collision never change its motion.

Torque and equilibrium

  • $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$, magnitude $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, direction perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec r$ and $\vec F$ (right-hand rule).
  • A rigid body is in equilibrium only when BOTH the net external force is zero AND the net external torque is zero.

Moment of inertia (I)

Body (about symmetry axis)I
Ring / hoop$MR^2$
Disc / solid cylinder$\frac12MR^2$
Solid sphere (about a diameter)$\frac25MR^2$
Thin rod (centre, ⊥ to length)$\frac{1}{12}ML^2$
  • Radius of gyration $k$ is defined by $I = Mk^2$.
  • Parallel axis theorem: $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$. Perpendicular axis theorem (planar lamina only): $I_z = I_x+I_y$.

Rotational dynamics

  • $\tau = I\alpha$ (the rotational analogue of $F=ma$).
  • Angular momentum $L = I\omega$; with zero external torque, $L$ is conserved: $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$ — e.g. a spinning skater speeds up when pulling her arms in ($I$ decreases).
  • Rotational kinetic energy $= \frac12I\omega^2$.

Rolling without slipping

  • $v = R\omega$; total KE $= \frac12mv^2\left(1+\dfrac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$, e.g. $\frac{7}{10}mv^2$ for a solid sphere, $\frac34mv^2$ for a disc.

Exam tip

KCET sets about 2–3 questions from this chapter, usually one moment-of-inertia lookup/combination and one torque, equilibrium, or angular-momentum-conservation numerical. Memorise the I-table exactly — most mistakes come from mixing up the formulas.

questions.q: Two point masses 2 kg and 3 kg are placed at $x = 0$ and $x = 5$ m respectively on the x-axis. The x-coordinate of their centre of mass is
questions.explanation: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{2\times0 + 3\times5}{2+3} = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3$ m.
questions.trick: $x_{cm}=\sum m_ix_i/\sum m_i$ — weighted average of positions.

questions.q: A force of 10 N is applied at a perpendicular distance of 0.5 m from a pivot. The torque produced is
questions.explanation: $\tau = F\times(\text{perpendicular distance}) = 10\times0.5 = 5$ N m.
questions.trick: $\tau=F\times r_\perp$ — direct plug-in.

questions.q: A ring of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m has a moment of inertia about its central axis (perpendicular to its plane) equal to
questions.explanation: For a ring, $I = MR^2 = 2\times(0.5)^2 = 0.5$ kg m$^2$.
questions.trick: Ring: $I=MR^2$ — memorise the I-table.

questions.q: A disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m has a moment of inertia about its central axis equal to
questions.explanation: For a disc, $I = \frac12MR^2 = \frac12\times2\times0.25 = 0.25$ kg m$^2$.
questions.trick: Disc: $I=\frac12MR^2$ — memorise the I-table.

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about a diameter is
questions.explanation: This is a standard result for a uniform solid sphere about its diameter: $I = \frac25MR^2$.
questions.trick: Solid sphere about diameter: $I=\frac25MR^2$ — memorise.

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform thin rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to its length, is
questions.explanation: Standard result for a thin rod about its centre: $I = \dfrac{ML^2}{12}$.
questions.trick: Thin rod about centre: $I=\dfrac{ML^2}{12}$ — memorise.

questions.q: A body has a moment of inertia of 0.2 kg m$^2$ about an axis through its centre of mass. Its moment of inertia about a parallel axis 0.5 m away, for a mass of 2 kg, is
questions.explanation: Parallel axis theorem: $I = I_{cm}+Md^2 = 0.2 + 2\times(0.5)^2 = 0.2+0.5 = 0.7$ kg m$^2$.
questions.trick: Parallel axis theorem: $I=I_{cm}+Md^2$.

questions.q: The perpendicular axis theorem ($I_z = I_x+I_y$) can be applied only to
questions.explanation: The perpendicular axis theorem is valid only for flat, plane laminas, not for general 3-D bodies like spheres or cylinders.
questions.trick: Perpendicular axis theorem applies only to flat (2-D) laminas.

questions.q: A body of moment of inertia 2 kg m$^2$ rotates with an angular velocity of 5 rad s$^{-1}$. Its angular momentum is
questions.explanation: $L = I\omega = 2\times5 = 10$ kg m$^2$ s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: $L=I\omega$ — direct plug-in.

questions.q: A spinning ice skater pulls her arms inward. As a result
questions.explanation: No external torque acts, so angular momentum $L=I\omega$ is conserved. Pulling arms in decreases $I$, so $\omega$ must increase to keep $L$ constant.
questions.trick: No external torque → $L$ conserved: $I$ down means $\omega$ up.

questions.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 4 kg m$^2$ rotates with angular velocity 3 rad s$^{-1}$. Its rotational kinetic energy is
questions.explanation: $KE_{rot} = \frac12I\omega^2 = \frac12\times4\times9 = 18$ J.
questions.trick: Rotational KE: $\frac12I\omega^2$ — direct plug-in.

questions.q: A torque of 10 N m acts on a body of moment of inertia 2 kg m$^2$. The angular acceleration produced is
questions.explanation: $\tau = I\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = \tau/I = 10/2 = 5$ rad s$^{-2}$.
questions.trick: $\tau=I\alpha\Rightarrow\alpha=\tau/I$.

questions.q: The condition for a wheel of radius $R$ to roll without slipping is that its centre-of-mass speed $v$ and angular velocity $\omega$ satisfy
questions.explanation: Rolling without slipping requires the contact point's velocity to be zero, giving $v = R\omega$.
questions.trick: Rolling without slipping: $v=R\omega$ — memorise this link.

questions.q: The total kinetic energy of a solid sphere of mass $m$ rolling without slipping with centre-of-mass speed $v$ is
questions.explanation: $KE = \frac12mv^2 + \frac12I\omega^2 = \frac12mv^2\left(1+\dfrac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$; for a solid sphere $k^2/R^2 = 2/5$, giving $KE = \frac{7}{10}mv^2$.
questions.trick: Solid sphere rolling KE $=\frac{7}{10}mv^2$ — memorise the rolling-KE table.

questions.q: A body of mass 2 kg has a moment of inertia of 8 kg m$^2$ about a given axis. Its radius of gyration about that axis is
questions.explanation: $I = Mk^2 \Rightarrow k = \sqrt{I/M} = \sqrt{8/2} = \sqrt4 = 2$ m.
questions.trick: Radius of gyration: $k=\sqrt{I/M}$.

questions.q: The torque $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ acting on a particle is directed
options: along the resultant of $\vec r$ and $\vec F$
perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec r$ and $\vec F$
questions.explanation: The cross product of two vectors is always perpendicular to the plane containing them, direction given by the right-hand rule.
questions.trick: Cross product $\vec r\times\vec F$ is always perpendicular to both vectors' plane.

questions.q: A rotating disc of moment of inertia 6 kg m$^2$ spinning at 2 rad s$^{-1}$ deforms (with no external torque) so that its moment of inertia becomes 3 kg m$^2$. Its new angular velocity is
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2 \Rightarrow 6\times2 = 3\times\omega_2 \Rightarrow \omega_2 = 4$ rad s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Angular momentum conserved: $I_1\omega_1=I_2\omega_2$.

questions.q: A shell at rest in mid-air explodes into several fragments purely under internal forces. The centre of mass of all the fragments
options: moves off in a new direction determined by the explosion
continues to fall along the same trajectory as if no explosion had occurred
stops instantaneously at the point of explosion
questions.explanation: Internal forces cannot change the motion of the centre of mass; only gravity (an external force) continues to act, so the COM keeps falling exactly as before.
questions.trick: Internal explosion forces can't change COM motion — it keeps falling as before.

questions.q: A rigid body is said to be in mechanical equilibrium when
options: only the net external torque on it is zero
only the net external force on it is zero
the body is necessarily at rest
both the net external force and the net external torque on it are zero
questions.explanation: Translational equilibrium requires zero net force; rotational equilibrium requires zero net torque. Both are needed together; the body could still be moving with constant velocity.
questions.trick: Equilibrium needs BOTH net force = 0 AND net torque = 0.

questions.q: A ring and a disc have the same mass and the same radius. Compared to the disc, the moment of inertia of the ring about the central axis perpendicular to its plane is
questions.explanation: $I_{ring} = MR^2$ while $I_{disc} = \frac12MR^2$, so the ring's moment of inertia is exactly twice the disc's.
questions.trick: Same mass & radius: $I_{ring}=2\times I_{disc}$ (memorise the ratio).

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a thin spherical shell (hollow sphere) of mass M and radius R about a diameter is
questions.explanation: For a thin hollow spherical shell about a diameter, $I = \frac23MR^2$ (larger than a solid sphere's $\frac25MR^2$ since the mass lies farther from the axis).
questions.trick: Hollow sphere about diameter: $I=\frac23MR^2$ (bigger than solid sphere's $\frac25$).

questions.q: Two point masses of 2 kg each are fixed at the two ends of a light rod of length 1 m. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to the rod, is
questions.explanation: Each mass is 0.5 m from the axis: $I = 2\times m(L/2)^2 = 2\times2\times(0.5)^2 = 1$ kg m².
questions.trick: Two point masses at rod ends: $I=2\times m(L/2)^2$, not $mL^2$.

questions.q: A particle of mass 2 kg moves in a straight line with speed 3 m s$^{-1}$. The perpendicular distance from a fixed point O to this line is 4 m. The angular momentum of the particle about O is
questions.explanation: For a particle in straight-line motion, $L = mvr_\perp = 2\times3\times4 = 24$ kg m² s$^{-1}$, and it stays constant since no torque acts about O.
questions.trick: Straight-line motion: $L=mv r_\perp$ (perpendicular distance to the line).

questions.q: A uniform disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m has moment of inertia 0.5 kg m² about the central axis perpendicular to its plane. Using the perpendicular axis theorem, its moment of inertia about a diameter is
questions.explanation: By symmetry $I_x=I_y$ for the two perpendicular diameters, and $I_x+I_y=I_z \Rightarrow I_x = I_z/2 = 0.5/2 = 0.25$ kg m².
questions.trick: Perpendicular axis theorem: by symmetry $I_x=I_y=I_z/2$ for a disc's diameter.

questions.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 5 kg m² spinning at 10 rad s$^{-1}$ is brought to rest in 5 s by a constant torque. The magnitude of the torque is
questions.explanation: $\alpha = \Delta\omega/t = 10/5 = 2$ rad s$^{-2}$; $\tau = I\alpha = 5\times2 = 10$ N m.
questions.trick: Find $\alpha=\Delta\omega/t$ first, then $\tau=I\alpha$.

questions.q: The SI unit of angular momentum is
questions.explanation: $L = I\omega$ has units kg m$^2$ $\times$ s$^{-1}$ = kg m$^2$ s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Angular momentum unit: kg m²/s (mass$\times$length²$\times$time⁻¹).

questions.q: A see-saw pivoted at its centre has a 30 kg child sitting 2 m from the pivot. For the see-saw to balance, a 20 kg child must sit on the other side at a distance of
questions.explanation: Balancing torques: $30\times2 = 20\times x \Rightarrow x = 3$ m.
questions.trick: Balance torques: $m_1r_1=m_2r_2$ about the pivot.

questions.q: A solid sphere rolls without slipping down a rough incline of angle 30°. Its linear acceleration is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+k^2/R^2} = \dfrac{10\times0.5}{1+2/5} = \dfrac{5}{1.4} \approx 3.57$ m s$^{-2}$.
questions.trick: Rolling acceleration down incline: $a=\dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+k^2/R^2}$.

questions.q: A ring, a disc and a solid sphere of the same mass and radius are released from rest together at the top of the same rough incline and roll down without slipping. The order in which they reach the bottom, fastest to slowest, is
questions.explanation: Acceleration $\propto 1/(1+k^2/R^2)$, which is largest for the sphere ($k^2/R^2=2/5$), then the disc ($1/2$), then the ring ($1$, the slowest).
questions.trick: Smaller $k^2/R^2$ rolls faster: sphere $<$ disc $<$ ring.

questions.q: A torque of 5 N m acts on a body, rotating it through one complete revolution ($2\pi$ rad). The work done by the torque is
questions.explanation: $W = \tau\theta = 5\times2\pi \approx 31.4$ J.
questions.trick: Rotational work: $W=\tau\theta$ (analogous to $W=Fd$).

questions.q: A couple is best described as
options: a pair of equal, opposite, parallel, non-collinear forces producing pure rotation without translation
a single force that produces rotation
any two forces acting on a rigid body
two equal and opposite forces acting along the same line
questions.explanation: A couple consists of two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide; it produces a net torque but zero net force, so it rotates the body without translating it.
questions.trick: A couple = equal, opposite, non-collinear forces → pure rotation, zero net force.

questions.q: For a rigid body rolling without slipping, the friction force at the point of contact with the ground is
options: zero, since the body is not sliding
static friction, since there is no relative sliding at the contact point
questions.explanation: The contact point is instantaneously at rest relative to the ground during rolling without slipping, so the friction acting there is static friction (though it may still be non-zero, e.g. down an incline).
questions.trick: Rolling without slipping → friction at contact is static, not kinetic.

questions.q: A rotating platform of moment of inertia 2 kg m² spins at 4 rad s$^{-1}$. A person then steps onto it, increasing the total moment of inertia to 4 kg m² (no external torque acts). The new angular velocity is
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2 \Rightarrow 2\times4 = 4\times\omega_2 \Rightarrow \omega_2 = 2$ rad s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: No external torque → $L$ conserved: $I_1\omega_1=I_2\omega_2$.

questions.q: A 1 kg mass moves at 2 m s$^{-1}$ and a 3 kg mass moves at 6 m s$^{-1}$, both in the same direction along the same line. The velocity of their centre of mass is
questions.trick: $v_{cm}=(m_1v_1+m_2v_2)/(m_1+m_2)$ — weighted average of velocities.

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a rigid body about a given axis depends on
options: only the total mass of the body
only the shape of the body
only the axis chosen, regardless of the mass
the mass and how it is distributed relative to the axis of rotation
questions.explanation: $I=\sum m_ir_i^2$ depends on both how much mass there is and how far each part lies from the chosen axis.
questions.trick: Moment of inertia depends on both mass AND its distribution about the axis.

questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass 3 kg and radius 0.2 m has a moment of inertia about its own (central, symmetry) axis equal to
questions.explanation: $I = \frac12MR^2 = \frac12\times3\times(0.2)^2 = 1.5\times0.04 = 0.06$ kg m².
questions.trick: Solid cylinder: $I=\frac12MR^2$, same formula as a disc.

questions.q: A disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m has a point mass of 1 kg attached at its rim, giving the system a moment of inertia of 0.5 kg m² about the disc's central axis. The torque needed to give it an angular acceleration of 4 rad s$^{-2}$ is
questions.explanation: $\tau = I\alpha = 0.5\times4 = 2$ N m.
questions.trick: Given combined $I$ already, just apply $\tau=I\alpha$ directly.

questions.q: The radius of gyration of a ring of radius R about its central axis (perpendicular to its plane) is
questions.explanation: Since $I_{ring}=MR^2=Mk^2$, the radius of gyration $k=R$: all the mass effectively acts at the rim itself.
questions.trick: Ring's radius of gyration equals its radius: $k=R$.

questions.q: In rotational motion, the quantity that plays the role analogous to mass (inertia) in linear motion is
questions.explanation: Moment of inertia measures a body's reluctance to change its rotational state, just as mass measures reluctance to change linear motion; compare $\tau=I\alpha$ with $F=ma$.
questions.trick: Moment of inertia is rotational analogue of mass — compare $\tau=I\alpha$ to $F=ma$.

questions.q: A uniform disc rolls without slipping such that its translational kinetic energy is 40 J. Its total kinetic energy (translational + rotational) is
questions.explanation: For a disc, $k^2/R^2=\frac12$, so total $KE = KE_{trans}(1+k^2/R^2) = 40\times1.5 = 60$ J.
questions.trick: Total rolling KE $=KE_{trans}(1+k^2/R^2)$; for disc, factor is 1.5.
